summary: Describes the optional AUTH command for POP3, which names an authentication mechanism, runs an exchange with the server, and can negotiate protection for later traffic. It has been replaced by RFC 5034.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1734 defines an optional POP3 AUTH command. It lets a client and server use a named authentication method and can also set protection for later messages on the connection.

questions: what does pop3 auth command do
subtitle: An optional POP3 command for choosing an authentication mechanism.

tldr.problem: POP3 needs a command for selecting an authentication mechanism and, optionally, agreeing on protection for later exchanges.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends AUTH with a mechanism name. The server and client exchange Base64-encoded challenges and answers, and may negotiate integrity and privacy protection.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1734 defines the earlier POP3 AUTH command and has been obsoleted by RFC 5034.

sections.title: Selecting an Authentication Method
sections.content:
The AUTH command names an authentication mechanism used by the POP3 client and server. The mechanism names and exchanges are based on those used by IMAP4, with pop used instead of imap in server authentication identities.

AUTH may be issued only in the AUTHORIZATION state, before the user has logged in. A server that does not support the requested mechanism should reject the command.
sections.plainLanguage: Before login, the client can ask the server to use a named authentication method. The server can reject a method it does not support.

sections.title: The Challenge and Answer Exchange
sections.content:
If the server supports the method, it sends challenges and the client sends answers specific to that method. A challenge is a line beginning with a plus sign and a space, followed by a Base64-encoded string; the client's answer is also Base64 encoded.

The client can cancel by sending a line containing a single asterisk. If authentication succeeds, the server sends a positive response and the session enters the TRANSACTION state.
sections.plainLanguage: The server and client exchange encoded messages defined by the chosen method. The client can cancel the exchange, and successful authentication moves the POP3 session into its transaction state.

sections.title: Optional Protection and Failed Attempts
sections.content:
An authentication method may also negotiate a protection mechanism that provides integrity and privacy for later traffic. If negotiated, it applies to all subsequent data on the connection and takes effect when the authentication exchange completes.

The RFC does not require a server to support a particular method or a method to provide protection. After a negative AUTH response, the session remains in AUTHORIZATION; the client may try another method or use USER/PASS or APOP.
sections.plainLanguage: Some methods can protect later messages from changes or disclosure. If an attempt fails, the client can try another method or another POP3 login command.

references.text: Myers, J., "IMAP4 Authentication Mechanisms", RFC 1731, Carnegie Mellon, December 1994.
